title: The rays bear the Sun aloft; the bright face of the gods has risen

words.meaning: who knows all that is born
the rays, the banners of light
to see, so that (all) may see

words.context: Bhāskara: «विश्वाय विश्वार्थं विश्वं लोको यथा एनं पश्येत्»

sandhi.rule: t before a vowel becomes d
final m before a stop becomes the nasal of its class (ñ before j, n before d)

samasa.vigraha: जातानि वेद इति, or जातं वेदः यस्य
samasa.meaning: who knows what is born; whose knowledge is born

morphology.note: a Vedic infinitive, the dative of the root noun दृश्; Bhāskara notes it as a listed form («'दृशे विख्ये च' इति निपात्यते»).
the dative of the pronominal विश्व without the pronominal ending -smai (Bhāskara: «स्मैभावाभावश्छान्दंसः»).

translation.literal: Up indeed that god, the knower of beings, the rays bear — the Sun, for all to see.
translation.readable: His rays lift up the god who knows all that is born — the Sun — so that the whole world may see him.

sandhi_exceptions.note: द्यावापृथिवी + अन्तरिक्षम्: a dual ending in ī is not joined to the following vowel (P. 1.1.11 (ईदूदेद्द्विवचनं प्रगृह्यम्)).

words.meaning: of the gods (or of the rays)

words.role: main verb of the first line

words.context: Bhāskara: «अनीकं सङ्घातरूपम्मण्डलम्», the disc as the gathering of the rays
Bhāskara: «रश्मिभिराप्राः आपूरयति», with a change of person («पुरुषव्यत्ययः»)

words.role: predicate: the Sun is the self

sandhi.rule: t before a vowel becomes d; m before c becomes ñ; -uḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -ur
-aḥ before a vowel other than a loses its visarga, leaving a hiatus

morphology.note: in a dvandva of deities दिव् takes the form द्यावा-; the dual ending -ī is the Vedic option for -yau (Bhāskara: «'वा छन्दसि' इति पूर्वसवर्णदीर्घः»).
the weak stem of the perfect participle of √स्था, ‘having stood’, i.e. what is stationary.

translation.literal: The bright face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, of Varuṇa, of Agni; it has filled heaven and earth and the mid-region: the Sun, the self of what moves and what stands still.
translation.readable: The bright face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa and Agni. It has filled heaven, earth and the air between: the Sun is the self of all that moves and all that stands.

meaning: Two famous verses on the rising Sun, recited together. In the first, the rays carry the Sun up into the sky so that everyone can see him. In the second, the Sun’s disc is the bright face of the gods and the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa and Agni; its light fills heaven, earth and the space between, and the Sun is called the self (ātman) of everything moving and unmoving. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā they stand together at 1.4.43.1; in the Ṛgveda they open two separate hymns to Sūrya, 1.50.1 and 1.115.1. Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara reads the second verse as teaching meditation on the Sun’s disc: «भवति मण्डलोपासनमिति».
in_the_rite: Midday sūryopasthāna: the third mantra (after ā satyena and ud vayam, before tac cakṣuḥ), recited standing and facing the Sun; it shares the viniyoga given for ā satyena in the Mylapore prayoga (vin-a-satyena).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara on the first verse: the rays bear the god up so that the whole world may see him — «विश्वार्थं, विश्वो लोको यथैनं पश्येदिति».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: On the second: the face is the disc, the gathering of the rays, «अनीकं सङ्घातरूपम्मण्डलम्»; it is the eye even of Mitra and the other gods, for they too see by its light — «मित्रादीनां देवानामपि चक्षुस्स्थानं , तेपि हि तेन प्रकाशितं पश्यन्ति»; and the Lord within the disc fills the worlds — «तदा तन्मण्डलान्तर्गतो भगवान् सूर्यः जगतो जङ्गमस्य तस्थुषः स्थावरस्य च विश्वस्यात्मा».

notes.label: linguistic
notes.text: The first verse is a gāyatrī, the second a triṣṭubh. The Ṛgveda (1.50.1, 1.115.1) has the same words; the Taittirīya spelling joins them (त्यञ्जातवेदसन्देवंवहन्ति).

notes.label: historical
notes.text: Ṛgveda 1.50 and 1.115 are the two great hymns to Sūrya in the first maṇḍala; ud vayam (1.50.10), recited just before in the rite, comes from the first of them.
